title: Splitting a number
objectives: Multiply a two-digit number by a one-digit number by splitting it into tens and units
Multiply by 11 and 12 with the grid method, keeping every partial product
Add the pieces as numbers, carrying where the tens overflow

screens.prose: A rectangle is 23 wide and 7 tall. A cut splits its width into 20 and 3.
screens.question: What is the area of the whole rectangle?

hints.text: Find the area of each piece first.
The left piece is 20 wide and 7 tall.
20 × 7 = 140 and 3 × 7 = 21. Add the two.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out each piece, then add the two areas.

byKey.missed-strip: You found the big piece, 140. The 3 by 7 strip adds 21 more.
byKey.strip-only: That is only the thin strip. Add the 20 by 7 piece, 140.
byKey.side-by-side: You wrote 14 and 21 side by side. Add the pieces instead: 140 + 21.
byKey.added-three: You added 3 to 140. The strip is 3 by 7, so it adds 21.
byKey.added: You added the width and the height. Area is width times height.

explain.text: The big piece is $20 \times 7 = 140$ and the strip is $3 \times 7 = 21$. Together they make $23 \times 7 = 161$. Both pieces are table facts, one with a zero on the end.

screens.prose: Same rectangle, 23 by 7, in one piece. Slide the cut anywhere. The caption works out both pieces for you.
screens.question: Which cut gives two pieces you can work out fastest in your head?

options.why: You cut near the middle. Then 12 × 7 and 11 × 7 both need their own working.
10 × 7 is easy, but 13 × 7 still needs splitting.
1 × 7 is easy, but 22 × 7 is no easier than 23 × 7.

hints.text: Which numbers are easy to multiply by 7?
A whole number of tens times 7 is a table fact with a zero on the end.

feedback.correct: A cut at a ten leaves a tens fact and a units fact.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a cut where both pieces are table facts.

explain.text: Every cut gives the same total, 161, because the rectangle never changes. Cutting at 20 makes both pieces table facts: $2 \times 7$ with a zero, and $3 \times 7$. That is the cut to reach for.

screens.prose: You cut 23 into tens and units, then multiplied each part by 7. That is **splitting**. Now split $47 \times 6$ the same way.
screens.question: Fill in both pieces and the total.

hints.text: The big piece is 40 by 6: four sixes with a zero on the end.
The thin strip is 7 by 6.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply each part of 47 by 6, then add.

byKey.r0c1: 40 × 6 is 4 × 6 = 24 with a zero on the end: 240.

explain.text: The pieces are 240 and 42, so $47 \times 6 = 282$. Start with the tens, so the biggest part is fixed first. Then add the small piece on.

screens.prose: Now $79 \times 8$. This time the two pieces carry when you add them.
screens.question: What is 79 × 8?

hints.text: Split 79 into 70 and 9.
The big piece is 70 by 8, which is 560.
560 + 72: 56 tens and 7 tens make 63 tens, then the 2. So 632.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find 70 × 8 and 9 × 8, then add them with care.

byKey.side-by-side: You wrote 56 and 72 side by side. The pieces must be added: 560 + 72.
byKey.dropped-carry: You added 6 tens and 7 tens but kept only 3 of them. 13 tens is 130, so the total is 632.
byKey.tens-only: That is just the big piece. Add the strip, 9 × 8 = 72.
byKey.rounded: That is 80 × 8. 79 is one less than 80, so take one 8 off: 632.

explain.text: In $560 + 72$ the tens are $6 + 7 = 13$, which carries a hundred. So $79 \times 8 = 632$. Add the pieces as numbers, never as strings of digits.

screens.prose: Both numbers can be split. Zetamac asks things like $12 \times 87$. Cut 12 into 10 and 2, and 87 into 80 and 7.
screens.question: Fill in the four pieces and the total.

hints.text: Each piece is its row label times its column label.
The bottom row is 2 tall: double 80 and double 7.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply each row label by each column label, then add all four.

explain.text: The top row is $10 \times 87 = 870$ and the bottom row is $2 \times 87 = 174$. Together they make 1044. Adding row by row is quicker than adding four pieces.

screens.prose: A shortcut for 11: write the two digits apart and put their sum between them. $11 \times 34$ gives 3, then $3 + 4 = 7$, then 4: 374. Try it on $11 \times 68$.
screens.question: What is 11 × 68?

hints.text: 6 + 8 is more than 9. Where does the extra ten go?
Split 11 into 10 and 1. The top piece is 10 × 68 = 680.
680 + 68 = 748. The 1 of the 14 carries into the hundreds.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split 11 into 10 and 1, and add the two pieces.

byKey.squeezed: You put 14 between 6 and 8. The middle place holds one digit, so the 1 carries: 6 + 1 = 7, giving 748.
byKey.dropped-carry: You kept the 4 of the 14 but dropped its 1. It carries into the hundreds: 748.
byKey.tens-only: That is 10 × 68 alone. Add one more 68.

explain.text: Splitting 11 into 10 and 1 gives $680 + 68 = 748$. The shortcut is that sum written fast, and $6 + 8 = 14$ carries a hundred. When the two digits add to 10 or more, carry the 1.

hints.text: How many pieces does the rectangle have?
Two pieces are not shaded.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count every piece of the rectangle.

byKey.ali: You agreed with Ali, who multiplied tens by tens and units by units. That leaves out two pieces: 10 × 7 and 2 × 40.
byKey.one-strip: You added 10 × 7 = 70 but not 2 × 40 = 80. Both unshaded pieces count.
byKey.other-strip: You added 2 × 40 = 80 but not 10 × 7 = 70. Both unshaded pieces count.

explain.text: Ali kept the two shaded pieces and lost the other two. $12 \times 47 = 400 + 70 + 80 + 14 = 564$. Splitting both numbers in two always gives four pieces.

screens.prose: Every time, you cut a number into parts and multiplied each part. For any numbers, $$(a + b) \times c = a \times c + b \times c$$ Now give a reason for each line of $86 \times 7$.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

hints.text: Which line still has 86 in it?
The bracket comes before it is multiplied out.
Split 86, multiply each part, work out the facts, then add.

feedback.correct: Split, multiply each part, then add.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the line that splits 86.

byKey.spread: That line multiplies out a bracket. Write the bracket first.
byKey.facts: Those two facts come from multiplying each part by 7.
byKey.add: That is the answer, so it comes last.

explain.text: Writing 86 as $80 + 6$ is the cut. Multiplying each part by 7 gives the two pieces, 560 and 42. Their tens make $6 + 4 = 10$, which carries a hundred: 602.

screens.prose: You buy 8 shares at £36.25 each. Split the price into £30, £6 and £0.25.
screens.question: What does the order cost, in pounds?

widget.label: Cost of the order in pounds

hints.text: Multiply each part of the price by 8.
8 lots of 25p is £2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply £30, £6 and £0.25 by 8, then add.

byKey.dropped-pence: You priced the shares at £36. The 25p on each of 8 shares adds £2.
byKey.pence-once: You added 25p once. Each of the 8 shares costs 25p more, which is £2 in all.

explain.text: The pieces are $8 \times 30 = 240$, $8 \times 6 = 48$ and $8 \times 0.25 = 2$. So the order costs £290.00. Splitting off the pence keeps the decimal point out of the way until the end.

ideas: Cut a number at a ten, multiply each part, then add: $23 \times 7 = 140 + 21$.
Split both numbers and you get four pieces. Every one of them counts.
Add the pieces as numbers and carry when the tens overflow: $560 + 72 = 632$.

formula.name: Splitting
formula.tex: (a + b) \times c = a \times c + b \times c
formula.note: With two splits, $(a + b)(c + d)$ has four pieces: $ac + ad + bc + bd$.

summary.trap: Tens times tens plus units times units drops two pieces: $12 \times 47$ is 564, not 414.

quiz.prose: Split the two-digit number into tens and units.
quiz.question: What is 7 × 86?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out 80 × 7 and 6 × 7, then add.

byKey.side-by-side: You wrote 56 and 42 side by side. Add 560 and 42 instead.
byKey.dropped-carry: The tens make 6 + 4 = 10, which carries a hundred. 560 + 42 = 602.

explain.text: $80 \times 7 = 560$ and $6 \times 7 = 42$. Adding, the tens make $6 + 4 = 10$, which carries a hundred: 602.

byKey.diagonal: You did 10 × 30 + 2 × 4. That drops two pieces: 10 × 4 and 2 × 30.

quiz.prose: Use the 11 shortcut, or split 11 into 10 and 1.
quiz.question: What is 11 × 79?

options.why: You put 16 between 7 and 9. Carry its 1 into the hundreds: 869.
You kept the 6 of the 16 and dropped its 1. It makes 7 + 1 = 8 hundreds.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out 10 × 79, then add one more 79.

explain.text: $790 + 79 = 869$. In the shortcut, $7 + 9 = 16$, so the 1 carries and 7 becomes 8. The answer reads 8, 6, 9.

quiz.prose: Four people split $9 \times 58$ into tens and units.
quiz.question: Whose working is right?

options.why: This person worked out $9 \times 5$ and dropped the zero. The tens part is $9 \times 50 = 450$.
This person added the 8 itself. The units piece is $9 \times 8 = 72$.
This person wrote 45 and 72 side by side. The pieces must be added.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply both parts of 58 by 9, then add.

explain.text: $58 = 50 + 8$, so $9 \times 58 = 450 + 72$. The tens make $5 + 7 = 12$, which carries a hundred: 522.
